questions.q: How do you confirm that the Hadamard matrix is unitary, given that it is real and symmetric?
options: Check that H has exactly two rows and two columns
Unitarity cannot be checked directly; it must be assumed
Check that H·H=I directly by matrix multiplication, since unitarity (U†U=I) reduces to U·U=I for a real symmetric matrix
Check that all entries of H are positive
questions.explain: For real symmetric matrices, the conjugate transpose equals the matrix itself, so U†U=I simplifies to U·U=I. Direct computation confirms H·H=I exactly for Hadamard.

questions.q: For the Hamiltonian H=(ħω/2)Z, what are the eigenstates and eigenvalues, and how are they found?
options: |0⟩ and |1⟩ both share the same eigenvalue, ħω
There are no eigenstates for this Hamiltonian
|+⟩ and |−⟩, both with eigenvalue 0
|0⟩ with eigenvalue +ħω/2 and |1⟩ with eigenvalue −ħω/2, found by applying H to each and using Z|0⟩=|0⟩, Z|1⟩=−|1⟩
questions.explain: Applying H to |0⟩ and |1⟩ using the known action of Z gives H|0⟩=(+ħω/2)|0⟩ and H|1⟩=(−ħω/2)|1⟩, identifying both as eigenstates with those respective eigenvalues.

questions.q: Why is the phase picked up by U(t)|0⟩ (a global phase) treated differently from the phase picked up by U(t)|+⟩ (a relative phase)?
options: There is no real difference; both effects are equally observable
Global phase only applies to multi-qubit states, never single qubits

|0⟩ has only one nonzero component, so any phase applies to the whole state uniformly and is unobservable; |+⟩ has two populated components whose phases can drift apart relative to each other, which is observable
Relative phase is always unobservable, just like global phase
questions.explain: The distinction depends on whether a phase affects every component of a state equally (global, invisible) or creates a difference between components (relative, physical) -- exactly what the |0⟩ vs |+⟩ comparison demonstrates with verified numbers.

questions.q: Why can't a non-unitary matrix represent valid quantum time evolution?
options: Non-unitary matrices are simply too large to represent a single qubit
Non-unitary matrices are forbidden purely by circuit-design convention, not by physics
A non-unitary matrix would cause a normalized input's total probability to drift away from 1 over time, violating the requirement that all outcome probabilities sum to 1
There is no actual restriction against non-unitary matrices as gates
questions.explain: Unitarity (U†U=I) is exactly what preserves ⟨ψ(t)|ψ(t)⟩=1 at every moment -- a direct consequence of the Schrödinger equation, not an arbitrary design rule.

questions.q: What does the verified identity S²=Z mean physically, in terms of time evolution?
options: If S corresponds to evolution under some Hamiltonian for duration t, applying S twice is physically the same as evolving under that Hamiltonian for duration 2t, and that doubled evolution happens to equal a Pauli-Z gate
It means applying S twice always returns the original input state unchanged
It means S is not a valid unitary gate
It means the S gate and the Z gate are actually unrelated operations that coincidentally share a symbol
questions.explain: Since gates are physically engineered durations of time evolution, applying the same gate twice corresponds to evolving for twice as long under the same underlying Hamiltonian -- S²=Z is the concrete, verified statement that this doubled duration matches the Z gate exactly.
